title: Every game, hundreds of pucks fly toward the net.
text:
Every game, hundreds of pucks fly toward the net.


But only some of them come from dangerous places.


A data story across 19 NHL seasons.




The Question
Since 2007, over 2 million shot attempts have been fired across the NHL. Some found the back of the net. Most didn’t. The data doesn’t lie — it maps out exactly where offense lives on the ice, and where it dies.
Where do the goals actually come from?




2M+


Total Shots




~140K


Goals Scored




19


Seasons Analyzed





Act I: The Big Picture
Zoom out. Every shot from every season, folded onto a single attacking end and overlaid on one rink. The bright spots reveal the hot zones — the areas where offense concentrates.
The glow is brightest between the faceoff circles, just above the goal line. This is the slot — the most dangerous real estate in hockey. The closer you are to the net, the more likely you are to score.
But not all players operate in the same neighborhoods.












  All 2.08 million shot attempts (shots, misses, and goals) from 19 seasons,
  folded onto a single attacking end. Brightest hexes sit in the slot, between
  the faceoff circles and above the goal line.




Act II: The Cast of Characters
Every position has its own shooting identity — but the real divide runs between forwards and defensemen.
Centers own the slot. They lurk in the high-traffic corridor right in front of the net, reading the play, waiting for the pass, and pouncing on loose pucks. About half of every center’s attempts come from inside the slot, and their heatmap is a concentrated glow right in the heart of the offensive zone.
Left Wings and Right Wings play the same game. Strip the names off the panels and their heatmaps are nearly indistinguishable from the centers’: the same neighborhoods, the same 30-foot average, the same 8% scoring rate. Mirror one wing’s map onto the other and they line up — there is no left side or right side of the ice here, just forwards camping on the same dangerous ground.
Defensemen shoot from everywhere — but especially from the point, near the blue line. Their job isn’t always to score. It’s to get pucks through traffic, create rebounds, and keep plays alive. Their shots come from about 20 feet farther out — nearly 50 feet on average — from wider angles, from places where goals are rare but chaos is abundant. They score on barely 3.5% of their attempts.
Every position plays a different game, but only two games are being played. The ice is not one story — it’s two.












  Each panel shows that position's own shot attempts as a share of its total,
  so the shapes are comparable across positions. Centers and both wings crowd
  the slot; defensemen load up at the point. The two wing maps are almost
  identical — forwards play one game, defensemen play another.













  Average shot distance by position, with each position's scoring rate.
  Defensemen fire from roughly 20 feet farther out — and score on fewer than
  half as many of their attempts as forwards do.




Act III: The Goal Line
Not all shots are created equal. A blast from the blue line and a tap-in from the crease are both “shots” — but they don’t score at the same rate.
The data makes this brutally clear. Shot density spreads across the entire offensive zone — wide, diffuse, hopeful. Goal density collapses into a tight cluster right in front of the net. The gap between where shots come from and where goals happen is the gap between hope and results.
Distance kills scoring chances. From the blue line, hundreds of shots yield almost no goals. From the crease, almost every shot is dangerous. The ice has a geography, and the goalies know it — but the shooters do, too.












  Left: every attempt as a share of all attempts. Right: every goal as a share
  of all goals — same color scale. Attempts smear across the whole zone; goals
  collapse into the slot. The slot holds 38.7% of attempts but 68.9% of goals.













  Scoring rate by shot distance across 19 seasons, with attempt counts inside
  each bar. Inside 10 feet, one in six attempts scores; from 50+ feet, it takes
  nearly 45 attempts for a goal.




The Takeaway
The NHL is a game of angles and inches. This data tells a clear story:

The slot is king. The area between the faceoff circles is where games are won.
Position dictates opportunity. Forwards camp in the slot and score on roughly 8% of their attempts. Defensemen create from a distance — 20 feet farther out, for about half the reward.
Proximity = probability. Every foot closer to the net dramatically increases your chance of scoring.

The ice surface hasn’t changed in a century. But how teams use it — that’s the game within the game.



Ready to dig deeper?


Head to the Exploration page to filter by season, position, and more.



  
    Shot data is sourced from MoneyPuck and
    covers all shot attempts (shots on goal, missed shots, and goals) from
    2007-2025. Both ends of the rink are folded onto one attacking end, with the
    net at x = 89. Scoring rate = goals divided by attempts.

title: When the Stands Went Empty
text:
On March 12, 2020, the puck stopped.
The season froze mid-stride. When it came back, the arenas were silent and the calendar looked nothing like before.
A data story about 2019-20, 2020-21, and what a crisis does to the record book.



Act I: The Interruption
The NHL’s heartbeat is a number: 1,230 regular-season games a year — later 1,271, then 1,312 as the league grew. The record book keeps the rhythm perfectly, which is exactly why the breaks stand out.
Three seasons broke it. In 2012-13, a lockout wiped out the first half of the schedule and the league squeezed 48 games into three months — just 720 in total. In 2019-20, the season stopped on March 12, 2020 with 1,082 of 1,271 games played: 189 games simply never happened. When play resumed that summer, it did so inside closed bubbles in Toronto and Edmonton — 24 teams, a qualification round nobody had planned for, and a playoff that ballooned to 130 games, more than 40 more than a typical spring.
Then came 2020-21: a 56-game schedule, division-only opponents, and 868 games played in near-silence.












  Regular-season games played by season. The three interrupted seasons are highlighted.





189


Games Never Played (2019-20)




130


Bubble Playoff Games




56


Games per Team (2020-21)





Act II: Silence in the Stands
Home ice was never just a phrase. The crowd, the last change, the wear of travel — across the seasons before the pandemic, home teams won about 54.7% of their games.
So what happens when you take the crowd away? In 2019-20, half its games were played in empty buildings; in 2020-21, almost all of them. Both seasons, home teams won exactly 53.3% of their games — a dip of nearly a point and a half from the old norm.
But notice what didn’t happen: home ice didn’t disappear. The edge thinned; it didn’t vanish. And the dip didn’t begin with the pandemic — 2018-19 had already slipped to 53.6%. The story the data tells is quieter than the mythology: a small, persistent home advantage, slightly dented, weathering the strangest conditions the league has ever played under.












  Home-team win rate in the regular season. Dashed line: the 2007-2018 average.
  The two pandemic seasons sit just below it — reduced, not erased.




Act III: A Different Kind of Season
2020-21 hockey felt different. A January start, a May finish, division-only opponents, almost no travel — teams played the same handful of rivals on back-to-back nights, over and over. The scoring sagged with it: 5.79 goals per game, down from 5.94 the year before and the lowest rate since 2016-17.
The shots changed shape, too. Attempts fell to about 60 per game, from roughly 63 a year earlier, while shooting percentage edged up to 9.66%. Fewer shots, slightly sharper ones, fewer goals — a grinding, defensive year produced by a schedule with no breathing room.
The pause, meanwhile, interrupted offense at its peak. Through 2019-20 the league was scoring 5.94 goals a game — the best rate in this dataset’s modern era up to that point. The lights went off at the wrong moment, and when they came back on, the goals didn’t come with them.












  Total goals per game in the regular season. Interrupted seasons are highlighted:
  2012-13 never moved the rate, but 2020-21 dipped.




Act IV: The Lesson in the Numbers
Shortened seasons were not new in 2020. The lockout year of 2012-13 produced 5.30 goals per game — wedged between 5.30 in 2011-12 and 5.33 in 2013-14. The lockout changed the calendar, not the game.
The same is true of the pandemic, down at the level of the ice itself. Look at where shots came from: in 2019-20 the average attempt launched from 35.8 feet, in 2020-21 from 35.1 — and their expected-goal value barely moved, 0.071 then 0.072. Both seasons sit right on the long trend line. The pandemic didn’t change where shots came from. The ice stayed the ice.
The real shift came after: by 2021-22, shots were more than a foot closer and worth measurably more — but that is a different evolution, one the pause didn’t cause.












  Where shots come from: average distance and expected-goal value of every shot
  attempt. The pandemic seasons follow the trend; the break comes after.



So here is the rule for reading this record: rate stats survive a crisis — counting stats don’t. Strip out 189 games and every leaderboard, point total, and save count is built on a different foundation than the seasons around it. Per-game rates hold up. When you browse the seasons in the Exploration tab, remember that 2019 means 2019-20 and 2020 means 2020-21 — two seasons that don’t play by the usual rules.





53.3%


Home Wins, Both Seasons




5.79


Goals per Game (2020-21)




35.1 ft


Avg Shot Distance (2020-21)




The Takeaway
What did the pandemic mean for the league? The data answers in three parts:

The bubble held. 130 games played in isolation, a full playoff completed safely — the template every other sports league rushed to copy.
Home ice thinned but survived. Empty buildings cost home teams about a point and a half of win rate — real, but far short of the edge’s disappearance.
The calendar broke; the game didn’t. Goals, distances, and expected values all stayed on trend. It was the schedule — never the ice — that the crisis rearranged.

And rearranged it for good: the division-only realignment invented out of necessity in 2020-21 became permanent, the revenue hole froze the salary cap for years, and the league that emerged kept a new appreciation for how much of the game lives in the numbers.



See it for yourself.


Head to the Exploration page and pull up seasons 2019 and 2020 alongside every other year.



  
    Shot data is sourced from MoneyPuck.
    Seasons are labeled by start year: 2019 = 2019-20, 2020 = 2020-21,
    2012 = 2012-13. Playoff game counts include the 2020 qualification and
    round-robin rounds.

title: The 2012 Lockout
text:
The season that almost wasn’t.


113 days of labor war. 510 games erased. A 48-game sprint from January to April.


The 2012–13 NHL lockout, and what the shot data shows.




What Happened
At 11:59 p.m. on September 15, 2012, the NHL’s collective bargaining agreement expired — and the owners locked out the players. It was the third lockout under commissioner Gary Bettman, and the fight was over the same fault line as always: money. Players had been taking roughly 57% of hockey-related revenue — a pool worth about $3.3 billion a year — while owners pushed for a 50–50 divide and a tighter salary cap.
The season was supposed to open on October 11. Instead, the calendar melted away. Preseason games canceled first, then regular-season games in waves, then the Winter Classic — the league’s outdoor showcase — and the All-Star Weekend. In total, 510 regular-season games never happened: 41.5% of the schedule.
Talks sputtered, broke down over the winter holiday, and nearly ended in court when the union considered disclaiming interest. Then, after a 16-hour bargaining session brokered by federal mediator Scot Beckenbaugh, a tentative deal landed at 4:45 a.m. on January 6, 2013 — 113 days after the lockout began. The new CBA split revenue 50–50, limited contract lengths, and was ratified within the week.




48


Games Per Team (vs. 82)




510


Games Never Played




5.30


Goals per Game — Unchanged from 5.30





The Sprint
The deal resurrected a 48-game season that ran from January 19 to April 28, 2013 — 99 days, roughly a game every other day. With no time to waste, the league scrapped all inter-conference games to cut travel and packed the schedule with back-to-backs after a one-week training camp.
The compressed chaos suited Chicago. The Blackhawks opened the season with 24 consecutive games without a regulation loss — an NHL record — and went on to win the Cup in June. The rest of the league simply tried to survive the treadmill.



By the Numbers
What did half a season do to the way the game was played? Almost nothing, at least per game. The shortened season produced 58.3 shots per game versus 59.5 the year before — a 2% dip — and scoring was essentially frozen at 5.30 goals per game in both seasons.
The lockout cut the quantity of hockey, not its character. Rate stats — the ones that describe how a game actually looks — shrugged off the disruption entirely.


Pace Held, Volume Vanished










  Shot and goal rates per game, computed from the MoneyPuck shot data.



```{=html}

The Deepest Dip in 19 Seasons










  Regular-season games per season from the shot data. The 2019-20 and 2020-21 dips are COVID-shortened seasons.
  Compare seasons interactively →




The Takeaway

The calendar shrank; the game didn’t. Shot and goal rates per game were nearly identical on either side of the lockout.
Half the sample. Any comparison involving 2012-13 rests on 720 games instead of 1,230 — read raw totals carefully.
Only a pandemic matched it. Across 19 seasons, only the COVID interruptions produced a comparable hole in the schedule.

The ice didn’t change when the lawyers left the room. Hockey, it turns out, is remarkably resistant to interruptions — as long as there are still games to play.



See it for yourself.


Head to the Exploration page and select season 2012 to explore the shortened year.
